metadata.title: Digital ambitions vs. classroom reality in Norwegian lower secondary schools: What digital competencies are students developing over time?

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This study is based on a longitudinal naturalistic video study of English lessons in Norwegian lower secondary schools (Years 9–10), using 29 recorded lessons split into 15-minute ICT segments (76 ICT segments). The paper does not report the use of any ILSA-style sampling weights (e.g., student/school design weights) or replicate-weight procedures, and the analysis is not framed as a population-representative survey estimation. Because the dependent variables are coded observation outcomes from video segments using the Norwegian Framework for Digital Skills (NDET, 2017b), weighting is not described as part of the estimation strategy. The main preprocessing steps are video segmentation (15-minute segments), exclusion of segments where ICT was not actually used (e.g., ICT for presentations or unused computers), and interrater reliability checks via double-coding of 20% of the material.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values are not applicable because the study does not use ILSA cognitive achievement scales with PV-based scoring; instead, it codes observed digital-skill opportunities and levels from video segments using the NDET (2017b) framework. Missing-data handling is not reported because the analysis is based on observational coding of video segments after explicit inclusion/exclusion of ICT-relevant segments, rather than statistical imputation of missing questionnaire or test responses.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic dataset consists of 29 video-recorded English lessons across five Norwegian lower secondary schools over 2019–23, split into 15-minute segments. First, the authors identified 24 English lessons containing any ICT-related activity (ICT lessons) and then split these into 15-minute ICT segments, yielding 76 ICT segments. Segments were excluded when the teacher used ICT only for presentations or when students had computers on their desks but were not using them. The study further zooms in on one case school (S07) for the later cohorts (2021–23), but the overall coding framework and segment-level scoring procedure remain the same.

data.outcome_summary: This paper reports a longitudinal, naturalistic video study of English teaching in Norwegian lower secondary schools (Years 9–10, ages 13–15) rather than an ILSA-based predictive modeling study. Across 29 recorded lessons, the authors identified 24 ICT lessons and coded 76 15-minute ICT segments using the Norwegian Framework for Digital Skills (NDET, 2017b), scoring each segment on five digital subskills (levels 1–5) and selecting the most advanced level when multiple were observed. The results show a “digital divide” across five schools in 2019–20: three schools provided frequent, multi-subskill opportunities (scored in 75%–100% of segments) while two schools provided infrequent opportunities (35%–50%), with no observed digital responsibility. When revisiting one school three years later (2021–23), opportunities increased substantially (e.g., ICT segments rising to 89%), but opportunities to develop beyond basic digital skills remained limited, with only rare advanced-level evidence. The study is limited by reliance on what is visible/expressed in video recordings and by the absence of survey-weighted, PV-based achievement outcomes.
data.null_fields_interpretation: The article is an observational longitudinal case study using video coding and a predefined digital-skills observation framework (NDET, 2017b). It does not conduct machine-learning model training/prediction, does not use ILSA/PISA/TIMSS/PIRLS-style plausible values, and does not report survey-weighted estimation or per-country sample sizes. Therefore, fields related to ML techniques, PV handling, and predictive performance metrics are not populated.
